# Camp hygiene and army health (`military_camp_hygiene`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by sanitation_sewerage, boiled_water, typhus_lice, contagion_theory, scurvy_citrus, quarantine
- Core idea: In many pre-industrial campaigns disease killed more soldiers than combat, above all dysentery, typhoid and typhus, and above all in sieges and standing camps. Dig latrines downhill and downstream, well away from the water point and the kitchens, and cover the waste with earth daily; draw drinking water upstream and boil it; move camp before the ground is fouled; keep men, clothes and bedding clean and free of lice; separate the sick; do not camp beside marshes.
- Pitfalls:
  - Blaming smell alone; a camp can smell clean and still drink its own sewage
  - Staying on one site for weeks, as besiegers must, without moving the latrines
  - Crowding the sick together with the healthy in tents and transports
  - Thinking wounds were the main risk; disease mortality could exceed combat mortality, and the proportions varied by campaign
- History: global: ancient Levant – Deuteronomy 23:12–14 orders latrines outside the camp and burial of excrement; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra places physicians with instruments and medicines behind the battle line; rome: 1st c. BC onwards – planned camps with latrines, drains and later hospitals (valetudinaria); c. AD 400 – Vegetius III.2 on water, camp sites and moving camp; islamic: 1683 – dysentery in the crowded Ottoman camp and in besieged Vienna alike; europe: 1752 – John Pringle, Observations on the Diseases of the Army; 1850s – Crimean War sanitary reforms; east_asia: 1904–1905 – Japanese army in the Russo-Japanese War cited as an early case of fewer deaths from disease than from battle
- Read:
  - Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris III.2
  - John Pringle, Observations on the Diseases of the Army (1752)
  - Hans Zinsser, Rats, Lice and History (1935)
